name: Gurr-goni
confidence_why: Green's 1995 reference grammar of Gurr-goni places primary stress on the first syllable of the root with secondary stress on prefixes and explains the second-syllable cases as unstressed fossilised prefixes, and the only other classification, Goedemans 1998 reporting Elwell's unpublished 1977 sketch as 'initial stress with very frequent stress on second, no regularities discovered', describes the same surface facts without an analysis.
catalog_citation: Green, Rebecca. 1995. A grammar of Gurr-goni (North Central Arnhem Land). PhD thesis, Australian National University, Canberra. xvi+352 pp. Open access: ANU Open Research, hdl 1885/9278.
catalog_locator: Ch. 1, section 1.2.2 'Stress', thesis p. 18; apparent exceptions, loans and stress shift pp. 18-20 page 35 also rendered and read as an image.
catalog_quote: Stress in Gurr-goni is to a large degree grammatically predictable: it is placed on the first syllable of the root. (Primary stress is shown here by an acute accent ´ placed before the stressed syllable.) Where the root takes prefixes, the first syllable of the prefix, or series of prefixes, takes secondary stress (shown here as ˝): ... In compound stems, formed of two or more roots, the first syllable of the first root may receive primary stress, while the first syllable of the second root takes secondary stress. This is so both for (many) reduplicated forms, and for other compounds ... Often, however, compound forms (but not reduplicated forms), have the primary stress on the first syllable of the second root, and secondary stress on the first. For some stems, this may be optional ...; for others, particularly derived verbs lexicalised with a particular meaning, stress placement appears to be fixed ... There are a large number [fn 10: 69, in a vocabulary of approximately 1200] of apparent exceptions to this rule of placing stress on the first syllable of the first root. Almost all of these probably contain a non-productive, unstressed, derivational or other prefix preceding the primary root (or, in some cases, a still productive prefix before a root that does not otherwise occur).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the root (root-initial, morphologically determined); in unprefixed words this is word-initial. Prefix strings carry secondary stress on their first syllable. In compounds and reduplications primary stress is on the first root and secondary on the second, though lexicalised compounds often reverse this.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable of the prefix (or prefix series); in compounds/reduplications, secondary stress on the first syllable of whichever root does not carry primary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: 69 apparent exceptions in a vocabulary of ~1200, almost all analysable as containing a frozen unstressed prefix (bV-, gV-, mV-, nu-, na-) or as old compounds; Kuninjku loans (nawaran 'python', manberg 'uplands') stress the borrowed prefix; stress shifts from monosyllabic root wu 'give' onto a preceding prefix syllable -bu-, and may shift onto the pronominal prefix before ni 'sit' in the zero-suffixed Precontemporary/Irrealis 2 tenses.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress described relative to morphological structure (root vs prefixes); examples are inflected verb and noun words in citation. Author's orthographic convention (p. 34): primary stress marked only where not obvious, i.e. not the first syllable or the first syllable after a prefix hyphen.
new_statements.identity_note: Green 1995 describes Gurr-goni (= Glottolog Guragone gura1252, ISO gge; older spelling Gungurugoni in Elwell 1977, Gurrgoni in StressTyp). Single variety; c. 1200-item vocabulary.

readall_conflicts: No new source was opened, so no new disagreement. The only tension on record is between the second-hand original-StressTyp classification of Gurrgoni (Goedemans 1998 App. D p. 244, from Elwell 1977: 'Initial stress with very frequent stress on second, no regularities discovered') and Green 1995's rule (primary stress on the first syllable of the root, secondary stress on the first syllable of a prefix string; ch. 1 sec. 1.2.2 pp. 18-20). Green's account explains the second-syllable cases: of about 1200 vocabulary items, 69 apparent exceptions almost all carry an unstressed fossilised prefix (bV-, gV-, mV-, nu-, na-) before the stressed root, and compounds may stress the second root. So the two are compatible once stress is counted from the root rather than the word edge; the StressTyp/Elwell classification is coarser, not contradictory. StressTyp2 itself says nothing.
